n: A royal psalm, probably used when a king of Israel was crowned. It asks why nations rage against God in useless rebellion. The New Testament applies it to Jesus Christ.

f.g: Plot something empty and doomed to fail.

n: Earthly kings and rulers band together against the Lord and his anointed king.

f.g: Hebrew mashiach (Messiah); Greek christos (Christ). Kings were anointed with oil.

n: They say, “Let’s break free of their chains and throw off their ropes” — rejecting God’s rule as if it were slavery.

f.g: Bonds, fetters — the yoke of God’s rule.

n: God, enthroned in heaven, laughs at their plotting. Their rebellion is no real threat to him.
Then he speaks to them in anger and terrifies them in his fury.
God declares that he has installed his own king on Zion, his holy mountain in Jerusalem.

f.g: The hill of Jerusalem where the temple stood.

n: The king announces God’s decree: “You are my Son; today I have become your Father.” Every Davidic king was called God’s son at coronation; the New Testament sees its fulfillment in Christ.

f.w: Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee

n: God promises the king the nations and the ends of the earth as his inheritance.

f.w: the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession

n: He will rule them with an iron scepter and shatter rebellion like clay pottery.

f.g: An iron scepter — unbreakable authority. Lehi’s and Nephi’s “rod of iron” is the word of God.

n: The psalm now urges the world’s kings to be wise and accept correction.
Serve the Lord with reverence and rejoice before him with awe.
Pay homage to the Son, the king, before his anger flares. All who take refuge in him are blessed. Christians see the Son as Jesus Christ.

f.g: Kissing was a sign of homage and submission to a king.

f.w: Blessed are all they that put their trust in him
